review.detail: The core carries the printed hypotheses, references, and sampling setting. The required $N_r$ exists by logarithmic versus polynomial growth. For $n\ge N_r$, the bounds $L\le(\log n)^\alpha$ and $(m-1)/(n-1)\le n^{-1/2}$ establish the capture condition. Combining the two lemmas gives low-degree mass at most $2rm^{-1/4}I_p(f)\le2rI_p(f)/(\log n)^\alpha$. Independently, Parseval bounds the remaining mass by $\sigma^2 I_p(f)/L$, where $\sigma^2/L=(64r)^\alpha\sigma^{2-\alpha}/(\log m)^\alpha\le(192r)^\alpha/(\log n)^\alpha$. This also covers $L<1$. For $r\le n<N_r$, Parseval gives $\Var_p(f)\le I_p(f)/4$, so the displayed choice of $C_r$ proves the assertion uniformly in $p$ and $f$.

paper.title: A uniform influence bound for hypergraph properties
paper.html:
Abstract

For every fixed integer r≥3, we prove that every relabeling-invariant Boolean property of simple r-uniform hypergraphs on n vertices satisfies Varp​(f)≤Cr​Ip​(f)/(logn)r/(r−1). The constant depends only on r, and the bound holds uniformly for all 0<p<1 without a monotonicity assumption. For increasing properties, it gives the corresponding threshold-width bound with exponent r/(r−1), proving the hypergraph threshold-width conjecture of Friedgut and Kalai.

1 Introduction

Let r≥3 and n≥r be integers, write [n]={1,…,n}, and put En,r​=(r[n]​). An element of {0,1}En,r​ represents a simple r-uniform hypergraph. A hypergraph property is a Boolean function on this space that is invariant under every permutation of [n]. For 0<p<1, give the coordinates the independent Bernoulli(p) law, and denote expectation and variance by Ep​ and Varp​.
For an edge e, let xe←b​ be x with its e-coordinate set to b. Define the pivotal influence of e and the total influence of f by
Ie,p​(f)=pPr​(f(xe←1​)=f(xe←0​)),Ip​(f)=e∈En,r​∑​Ie,p​(f).
The probability in the first expression is over the other coordinates; it does not include an additional factor of p(1−p). All logarithms are natural, and n always counts vertices.
Theorem 1.1.
For every integer r≥3 there is a finite constant Cr​ such that, for every integer n≥r, every 0<p<1, and every hypergraph property f:{0,1}En,r​→{0,1},
Varp​(f)≤(logn)r/(r−1)Cr​​Ip​(f).(1.1)
No monotonicity assumption is required.
The theorem measures how vertex symmetry forces sensitivity to edge changes. If the probability of a property stays bounded away from zero and one, its total influence must grow at least as (logn)r/(r−1).
A property is increasing if changing coordinates from 0 to 1 cannot decrease its value, and nontrivial if it is not constant. For a nontrivial increasing property, put q(p)=Ep​f and define pa​=inf{p∈[0,1]:q(p)≥a} for 0<a<1. For fixed 0<ε<1/2, its threshold width is p1−ε​−pε​. Friedgut and Kalai conjectured that this width is at most Or,ε​((logn)−r/(r−1)) for every increasing r-uniform hypergraph property [5, Section~5, p.~2999]. Their formulation counts edge coordinates rather than vertices; for fixed r, log(rn​)∼rlogn as n→∞. Corollary 4.1 proves this conjectured bound by integrating (1.1), with an explicit dependence on ε.
Context and attribution. Kahn, Kalai, and Linial [6] established a fundamental link between Fourier analysis and the influences of Boolean functions. For a function invariant under a transitive group on M coordinates, their theorem gives a total-influence lower bound of order Var1/2​(f)logM at the uniform measure. Bourgain, Kahn, Kalai, Katznelson, and Linial [3] extended the influence method to product spaces. Friedgut and Kalai [5] used influence inequalities to prove sharp thresholds for increasing families with transitive symmetry. For hypergraph properties, the induced action on the (rn​) edge coordinates is transitive. The richer structure of vertex permutations, however, contains more information than this single transitivity statement.
Bourgain and Kalai [4, Corollary~4.1] studied how group actions on sets of coordinates improve influence estimates. For fixed r and every η>0, their result gives a lower bound of order Var1/2​(f)(logn)r/(r−1)−η for the total influence of a hypergraph property at the uniform measure. Their influence results already allow nonmonotone functions. Kelman, Kindler, Lifshitz, Minzer, and Safra obtained further estimates for group-invariant functions [7]. For graph properties, these give I1/2​(f)≥cVar1/2​(f)(logn)2/(loglogn)2 for sufficiently large n; see the arXiv version cited in [7, Section~7.4]. The present proof uses vertex symmetry through restrictions: all edges touching a vertex block remain free, and only edges wholly outside the block are fixed. This is the method of the companion manuscript A Sharp Threshold Bound for Monotone Graph Properties [9, Theorem~1.2 and Sections~2--3], which establishes the corresponding variance bound with denominator (logn)2 for graph properties, uniformly in p and without monotonicity. We reproduce its Fourier estimate and restriction argument in full. The additional combinatorial step replaces the graph degree estimate by its r-uniform counterpart, producing the exponent r/(r−1).
Proof strategy. Put σ=p(1−p)​ and α=r/(r−1). The Fourier expansion for the Bernoulli product measure is indexed by sets S of hyperedges. Its squared nonconstant coefficients sum to the variance; weighting them by ∣S∣ gives σ2Ip​(f). Thus the influence controls high degrees. The task is to bound the remaining mass using symmetry.
For large n, choose a uniformly random block B of m vertices, with m about n​, and leave free all edges meeting B. Every permutation within B survives an assignment to the other coordinates, and every free-edge orbit has at least m elements. Section 2 bounds the restricted Fourier mass up to a degree k proportional to σlogm by m−1/4 times the restricted total influence. Its linear dependence on influence allows averaging over the assigned coordinates.
Regard a nonempty Fourier index S as an r-uniform hypergraph with s edges. It has a vertex of positive degree at most rs(r−1)/r. For s≤L=(k/r)α, this degree is at most k. The event that B meets the union of these edges only at that vertex has probability comparable to m/n and leaves between one and k support edges free. After averaging over the assignments and B, the restricted total influence is at most (rm/n)Ip​(f), so the two factors of m/n cancel. Section 3 thereby controls the original Fourier mass up to degree L.
Since L is of order (σlogn)α, the remaining mass is at most σ2Ip​(f)/L, with coefficient of order σ2−α(logn)−α. The positive exponent 2−α makes this bound uniform in p. Section 4 completes the estimate and derives the threshold consequence.

2 A Fourier estimate for small individual influences

We first work on an arbitrary finite coordinate set J. Our objective is to control low-degree Fourier mass when every individual influence is small relative to the total. We follow the elementary argument in [9, Lemma~2.1]; its analytic ingredient is a two-to-four norm estimate of the type underlying the classical hypercontractive inequalities [2; 1]. The proof below includes the dependence on the bias.
Fix 0<p<1 and put σ=p(1−p)​. For i∈J and A⊆J, define
χi​(x)=σxi​−p​,χA​(x)=i∈A∏​χi​(x),χ∅​=1.
Independence, zero means, and unit second moments show that the χA​ form an orthonormal basis. Write h(A)=Ep​[hχA​]. Throughout this section, norms and expectations use this product law, and Ii​(h) and I(h) denote pivotal and total influence on J.
For Boolean h, let Δi​h be the function on the other coordinates obtained by subtracting the section at xi​=0 from the section at xi​=1. Direct expectation in coordinate i gives
h(A∪{i})=σΔi​h​(A)(A⊆J∖{i}).
Because Δi​h∈{−1,0,1}, Parseval's identity yields
S⊆J∑​∣S∣h(S)2=σ2I(h),Varp​(h)=∅=S⊆J∑​h(S)2.(2.1)
In particular, this identity uses no sign condition on Δi​h.
Lemma 2.1 (Low-degree mass).
Let m≥2 be real and let h:{0,1}J→{0,1} satisfy Ii​(h)≤I(h)/m for every i∈J. With k=σlogm/64, one has
1≤∣S∣≤k∑​h(S)2≤m−1/4I(h).(2.2)
The sum is empty when k<1.
Proof.
We will use a two-to-four norm estimate to bound low-degree projections of the differences Δi​h. Set ρ=σ/4 and define the linear operator T by TχA​=ρ∣A∣χA​. We first prove
∥Tg∥4​≤∥g∥2​(2.3)
for every real-valued function g on the product space. For one coordinate, ∣χi​∣≤1/σ and Eχi2​=1 imply ∣Eχi3​∣≤1/σ and Eχi4​≤1/σ2. For real a,b, expansion and 2∣ab3∣≤a2b2+b4 give
E(a+ρbχi​)4​≤a4+6ρ2a2b2+σ2ρ3​(a2b2+b4)+σ2ρ4​b4=a4+3213σ2​a2b2+2569σ2​b4≤(a2+b2)2,​
where the last inequality uses σ≤1/2.
To extend this estimate to the product, induct on ∣J∣, starting with the constant functions when J is empty. Write g=a+bχi​, where a,b depend on the remaining coordinates, and use T for the operator on those coordinates as well. The one-coordinate estimate, applied pointwise, followed by the L2 triangle inequality gives
∥Tg∥42​≤∥(Ta)2+(Tb)2∥2​≤∥Ta∥42​+∥Tb∥42​≤∥a∥22​+∥b∥22​=∥g∥22​.
This proves (2.3).
Let P≤k​ be the orthogonal projection onto the span of χA​ with ∣A∣≤k. For every u in this span,
∥u∥4​≤∥T−1u∥2​≤ρ−k∥u∥2​.
Taking the supremum of ∣E[gu]∣ over unit L2 vectors in this span, and applying Hölder's inequality, therefore gives
∥P≤k​g∥2​≤ρ−k∥g∥4/3​.(2.4)
These inequalities are valid for real k≥0, with no rounding required.
Each nonempty Fourier support is counted at least once when summed over its coordinates. Using the difference identity and enlarging the resulting degree cutoff from k−1 to k, we obtain
1≤∣S∣≤k∑​h(S)2​≤σ2i∈J∑​∥P≤k​Δi​h∥22​≤σ2ρ−2ki∈J∑​Ii​(h)3/2.​(2.5)​
Here each projection acts on the coordinates other than i, and ∥Δi​h∥4/32​=Ii​(h)3/2 because ∣Δi​h∣ is an indicator.
The function σlog(4/σ) is increasing on (0,1/2] and is at most 2. Hence ρ−2k≤m1/16. If I(h)≤m1/4, then Ii​(h)1/2≤m−3/8, so (2.5) is at most σ2m−5/16I(h)≤m−1/4I(h). If I(h)>m1/4, the right side of (2.2) exceeds 1, whereas its left side is at most Varp​(h)≤1/4.
∎

3 Restriction to a vertex block

Return to a hypergraph property f on E=En,r​ and fix the bias p, with σ=p(1−p)​. Its Fourier coefficients use the basis of Section 2, with J=E. The restriction method of [9, Lemma~3.1 and Proposition~3.2] preserves a large permutation group after conditioning. We first obtain an averaged estimate for restricted Fourier degrees, and then relate those degrees to the sizes of the original supports.
For a vertex set B⊆[n], write
FB​={e∈E:e∩B=∅}
for the edge coordinates that remain free.
Lemma 3.1 (Averaged restriction estimate).
Let r+1≤m≤n be integers and set k=σlogm/64. For B chosen uniformly among the m-subsets of [n],
S⊆E∑​BPr​(1≤∣S∩FB​∣≤k)f​(S)2≤m−1/4nrm​Ip​(f).(3.1)
Proof.
Fix B and an assignment y to the coordinates in E∖FB​. Denote the resulting Boolean function on FB​ by fy​. Every permutation supported on B fixes each edge outside FB​ individually, and consequently fixes y. Thus fy​ is invariant under all these permutations, regardless of the assignment.
An edge with j vertices in B has an orbit of size (jm​): its outside part is fixed and its inside part can be any j-subset of B. Since 1≤j≤r<m, this size is at least m. The free product measure is invariant under the same permutations, so influences are equal within each orbit. It follows that
Ie​(fy​)≤I(fy​)/m(e∈FB​).
Lemma 2.1 therefore applies to every fy​.
Average its conclusion over the product law of y. For A⊆FB​, the Fourier expansion of f gives
fy​​(A)=D⊆E∖FB​∑​f​(A∪D)χD​(y).
Orthonormality in the assigned coordinates yields
Ey​[fy​​(A)2]=D⊆E∖FB​∑​f​(A∪D)2.
Also Ey​Ie​(fy​)=Ie,p​(f) for every e∈FB​, by conditioning the disagreement event. Consequently
S:1≤∣S∩FB​∣≤k∑​f​(S)2≤m−1/4e∈FB​∑​Ie,p​(f).
Finally average over B. For each fixed edge e, a union bound on its r vertices gives PrB​(e∈FB​)≤rm/n, proving (3.1).
∎
The next lemma extends the graph capture argument of [9, Lemma~3.3] to identify the hypergraph supports detected by this estimate. Here a support S is itself a set of distinct r-edges; its vertex union contains no isolated vertices.
Lemma 3.2 (Capturing a support at one vertex).
Let n≥r≥3 and 1≤m≤n be integers, let k>0, and put
α=r−1r​,L=(k/r)α.
Suppose
rLn−1m−1​≤21​.(3.2)
For a uniform m-subset B of [n] and every S⊆En,r​ with 1≤∣S∣≤L,
BPr​(1≤∣S∩FB​∣≤k)≥2nm​.(3.3)
Proof.
Fix such an S, write s=∣S∣, and let V=⋃e∈S​e and v=∣V∣. Because s≤(rv​)≤vr, the average degree of the hypergraph with edge set S is at most
vrs​≤rs(r−1)/r≤k.
Choose a vertex u∈V of degree dS​(u) between 1 and k. This choice depends only on S, before B is sampled.
Conditional on u∈B, each other vertex lies in B with probability (m−1)/(n−1). The union bound and v≤rs≤rL therefore give
BPr​(B∩V={u})​≥nm​(1−(v−1)n−1m−1​)≥2nm​.​
On this event, the edges of S meeting B are exactly those containing u. Thus ∣S∩FB​∣=dS​(u)∈[1,k].
∎
The captured set need not consist of a single edge: the block meets one support vertex, and retains every support edge incident with it. Also the vertex u may vary with S, since (3.3) is a separate probability bound for each nonnegative summand in (3.1).
Combining Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 gives, whenever their hypotheses hold,
1≤∣S∣≤L∑​f​(S)2≤2rm−1/4Ip​(f).(3.4)
If L<1, this conclusion holds because the sum is empty. Otherwise, restrict the nonnegative sum in (3.1) to 1≤∣S∣≤L and divide by the lower bound m/(2n). This completes the transfer from restricted degree k to original degree (k/r)r/(r−1).

4 The uniform bound and its threshold consequence

We now choose the block size so that (3.4) controls the low-degree part of the variance. The weighted Parseval identity will control the remaining degrees.
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Fix r≥3 and write α=r/(r−1). Choose an integer Nr​>r such that, for every n≥Nr​ and m=⌊n​⌋,
m≥r+1,logm≥31​logn,r(logn)αn−1/2≤21​,m−1/4(logn)α≤1.​(4.1)
Such an Nr​ exists: m is asymptotic to n​, and any fixed power of logn grows more slowly than a positive power of n. In particular, the choice is independent of p and f.
Assume first that n≥Nr​, and set
σ=p(1−p)​,k=64σlogm​,L=(k/r)α.
Both cutoffs are positive. Since k/r≤logn and
n−1m−1​≤n−1n​−1​=n​+11​≤n−1/2,
the third condition in (4.1) implies (3.2). Thus (3.4) and the fourth condition in (4.1) give
1≤∣S∣≤L∑​f​(S)2≤(logn)α2r​Ip​(f).(4.2)
For the remaining degrees, (2.1) gives
∣S∣>L∑​f​(S)2≤L1​S∑​∣S∣f​(S)2=Lσ2​Ip​(f).
The decisive bias dependence is
Lσ2​=(logm)α(64r)ασ2−α​≤(logn)α(192r)α​.(4.3)
Indeed 2−α=(r−2)/(r−1)>0, σ≤1, and logm≥(logn)/3. This estimate remains valid at arbitrarily small positive σ. If L<1, the low-degree sum is empty and the same tail estimate bounds the whole variance.
Adding the two parts proves (1.1) for n≥Nr​ with constant 2r+(192r)α. For r≤n<Nr​, (2.1) gives Varp​(f)≤σ2Ip​(f)≤Ip​(f)/4. Therefore a valid choice for all n and p is
Cr​=max{2r+(192r)α,4(logNr​)α​}.
∎
We finish with the threshold consequence stated in the introduction. Recall that q(p)=Ep​f and pa​=inf{p∈[0,1]:q(p)≥a}.
Corollary 4.1.
For a nontrivial increasing property of r-uniform hypergraphs on n≥r vertices, where r≥3, and every 0<ε<1/2,
p1−ε​−pε​≤(logn)r/(r−1)2Cr​​logε1−ε​.
Proof.
The Margulis–Russo identity relates pivotal influences to the probability derivative; see [8], [10, Lemma~3], and [5, Lemma~2.2]. Here it follows directly by giving each coordinate its own bias: the expectation is affine in each bias separately, and its partial derivative in coordinate e is Ep​[f(xe←1​)−f(xe←0​)]. Monotonicity identifies this with Ie,p​(f). Differentiating along the common bias gives q′(p)=Ip​(f).
Nontrivial monotonicity gives q(0)=0 and q(1)=1. Some pair of configurations differing in one coordinate has different values, so its pivotal event has positive probability for every 0<p<1. Hence q′(p)>0 there, and the stated quantiles exist uniquely. Theorem 1.1 implies
q(p)(1−q(p))q′(p)​≥Cr​(logn)r/(r−1)​.
Integrating from pε​ to p1−ε​, using the antiderivative log(q/(1−q)), proves the claim.
∎

Theorem 1.1, using Varp​(f)=q(p)(1−q(p)), gives the displayed differential inequality; its constant Cr​ is positive because the variance is positive. Integration gives 2log((1−ε)/ε) and precisely the claimed bound. The missing-hypotheses lint is dismissed: r≥3 and n≥r are explicit, and the entire integration interval lies in 0<p<1, where the core already supplies the product law.
